Leadership remains under the law

Joshua is a new commander facing a war. The LORD’s orders in verses 6–9 say almost nothing about tactics. Three times he says to be strong and courageous. In between, verse 8 gives one practice: keep the law in his mouth always. Success is tied to doing “all that is written in it.” This matches the rule for kings in Deuteronomy 17:18–19. Israel’s leader does not stand above the law he enforces.
The first witness comes from outside

The spies were sent to learn about Jericho. What they learn comes from Rahab’s mouth. She retells the Red Sea and the defeat of two kings (verses 9–10). Verse 11 calls the LORD “God in heaven above, and on earth beneath.” Moses used nearly the same words in Deuteronomy 4:39. So the first clear statement of faith in the land comes from a Canaanite woman. She then acts on it at risk to herself (verses 4–6 and 15).
The crossing gives the priests a public task

Verse 15 notes that the Jordan was in flood at harvest time. The river does not part while the people watch from the bank. Verse 13 ties the stopping to the priests’ feet resting in the water. They must step in while it is still running. Verse 17 has them stand in the riverbed until the whole nation is across. The priests go first and leave last. Verse 7 says the event also shows that God is with Joshua.
A memorial requires an explanation

A pile of stones says nothing without someone to speak for it. Verse 6 expects children to ask what the stones mean. Verse 7 gives parents the answer to pass on. The stones come from the exact place the priests stood (verse 3). So they are evidence as well as a marker. Verses 21–24 repeat the question and link the Jordan to the Red Sea. The aim reaches past Israel: that all peoples may know the LORD’s hand.
The commander changes Joshua's question

Joshua’s question in verse 13 offers two choices: for us or for our enemies. The man’s first word is “No.” He is not a soldier for either side to claim. He commands the LORD’s army, and Joshua is the one who must take a side. Joshua understands at once and falls on his face. He then asks the better question: what does his lord say? Verse 15 repeats what Moses heard at the bush (Exodus 3:5).
Destruction and rescue occupy the same account

The chapter gives Jericho’s fall in verse 20 and its destruction in verse 21. Verse 21 lists who died: men, women, young, and old. Verses 22–25 then tell of one house that was spared. The spies keep the oath of 2:14 and bring out Rahab’s whole family. Verse 25 gives the reason: “she hid the messengers.” A Canaanite woman now lives “in the middle of Israel.” The account sets rescue beside destruction and does not explain away either.
Hidden goods create a public crisis

Verse 1 blames “the children of Israel” for what one man did. Thirty-six soldiers die before anyone knows why (verse 5). Achan’s confession in verse 21 walks through the steps: saw, coveted, took. Then he hid the goods in the ground under his tent. What was buried in private had already cost lives in public. Verse 11 says the theft also involved deceit. The penalty falls on his household too, with no comment given (verses 24–25).
The law is heard beyond the fighting force

After two battles Joshua stops the war for a reading. Moses ordered this at Mount Ebal in Deuteronomy 27:2–8. Joshua builds the altar, writes the law on stones, and reads it all. Verse 34 says he read “the blessing and the curse.” Verse 35 names those who heard: women, little ones, and foreigners. None of these fought at Ai. The law belongs to the whole people, not only to its army.
An oath survives a failed decision

Verse 14 names Israel’s mistake: they tested the bread and did not ask the LORD. The covenant in verse 15 rests on a lie the Gibeonites told. Three days later the truth comes out. The leaders still say, “We have sworn to them by the LORD” (verse 19). An oath in God’s name binds them even though they were tricked. So the Gibeonites live, as servants at the altar (verse 27). Their reason in verse 24 is the same fear Rahab named in 2:9–11.
An agreement creates a duty in war

Gibeon won its treaty by a trick in chapter 9. Now the treaty brings an attack, and Gibeon calls for help (verse 6). Joshua could have let the kings remove a problem for him. He marches all night to keep the oath (verse 9). The LORD backs that choice with hail and a long day (verses 11–14). So this battle is fought for an ally Israel did not want. Second Samuel 21:1–2 later treats breaking this oath as a serious wrong.
The account preserves a long campaign

Chapters 10 and 11 can read like a quick sweep through the land. Verse 18 corrects that: “Joshua made war a long time.” Caleb’s words in 14:10 suggest several years had passed. Verse 13 adds that most cities were left standing, and only Hazor was burned. Verse 22 notes that some Anakim remained in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. So the summary “the whole land” in verse 23 has stated limits. Chapter 13:1 says much land still remained.
A list gives conquest a remembered shape

The chapter turns the battles of chapters 6–11 into a count. Each king gets the same short line and the word “one.” Verses 1–6 credit Moses with the eastern land. Verses 7–24 credit Joshua with the western land. Putting both together shows one work under two leaders. Each king is tied to one city, so the list is thirty-one towns. Chapter 13 then lists what was not yet taken.
A completed campaign is not complete possession

Chapter 11:23 said Joshua took the whole land. Verse 1 now says “very much land” remains. Both statements stand in the book. The kings were beaten, but many places were not yet lived in. Verses 2–6 name the gaps, and verse 13 names peoples left in place. The LORD tells Joshua to divide the land anyway (verse 7). Each tribe receives a share that it must still go and settle.
An earlier witness becomes a land claim

Forty-five years earlier ten spies feared the Anakim’s walled cities (Numbers 13:28–33). Caleb said Israel could take the land. In verse 12 he asks for that same hill country, giants and all. He does not ask for an easy share as a reward. His words are careful: “It may be that the LORD will be with me.” His claim rests on Moses’s oath in verse 9. The man who trusted the promise then asks to act on it now.
A land gift still needs water

Achsah is given in marriage as a prize for a battle (verses 16–17). In verses 18–19 she acts for herself. She gets off her donkey and speaks to her father directly. Her land is in the South, and she needs water for it. A field there is of little use without a spring. She asks for “a blessing” and names it: springs of water. Caleb gives her two, the upper and the lower.
Settlement includes dependence within shared towns

Most of the chapter is a border list. Verse 10 ends it with a failure and a result. Ephraim did not drive out the people of Gezer. The Canaanites stayed and became forced laborers. Israel once did forced labor in Egypt (Exodus 1:11). Now Israelites set that burden on others. The same note returns in 17:13 and in Judges 1:28–30.
A promised rule must reach actual families

Numbers 27:7 gave these five women a promise years earlier. A promise on record still has to be carried out when land is handed over. In verse 4 they come to the same kind of court as before. They quote the command: the LORD told Moses to give them a share. The leaders do not argue. Verse 6 shows the effect on the count of Manasseh’s portions. The rule made in the wilderness now reaches an actual family.
An allotment requires shared knowledge of land

Seven tribes are slow to move, and Joshua rebukes them (verse 3). His fix is practical. Men from each tribe must walk the land and describe it (verses 4, 8). Every tribe has its own surveyors, so no one divides it unseen. The written record comes back to Shiloh. There the shares are assigned by lot “before the LORD” (verse 10). People measure, and the lot decides who gets which part.
The leader receives his portion last

Chapters 14–19 hand out land tribe by tribe. Verse 49 says Joshua’s share comes when they “finished distributing.” The leader who ran the division takes his part last. He does not assign it to himself. The people give it, and verse 50 says it was by the LORD’s command. He asks for one town in his own tribe’s hills. Caleb opened the list of shares in chapter 14, and Joshua closes it.
Protection leaves room for a hearing

Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19 ordered these cities. Here they are named and placed across the land. Verse 4 has the man explain himself at the gate before he enters. Verse 5 protects him because he “didn’t hate him before.” The test is intent, shown by the past between the two. Verse 6 still requires a trial before the community. Verse 9 opens the cities to foreigners as well as Israelites.
Sacred service depends on other households

The Levites have no tribal territory (13:33). They must ask for what Moses promised them (verse 2). Verse 3 says the other tribes gave “out of their inheritance.” Every tribe loses some towns so the Levites can live. The towns are spread through all the tribes, not kept in one place. So those who serve at the sanctuary depend on every other household. Verse 45 then sums up the whole division: nothing the LORD promised failed.
A visible object can carry different meanings

The western tribes see an altar and assume rebellion (verses 11–12). A second altar would break the rule of one place for sacrifice. They arm for war but send men to ask first. The builders give a meaning no one had guessed. They feared the Jordan would one day cut their children off (verses 24–25). The altar is a copy to look at, not a place to offer (verse 28). Asking before attacking prevents a war between brothers.
The farewell names limits to future security

Joshua’s speech looks back at promises kept (verse 14). It also looks ahead with a condition. Verse 12 names the danger: clinging to the nations that remain. Verse 13 gives the result in four pictures: a snare, a trap, a scourge, thorns. The LORD’s help in war is not automatic. Verse 15 says the warnings are as sure as the blessings were. Judges 2:1–3 reports that this is what happened.
Land possession does not finish the story

The people already live in the land, and the wars are over. Verse 15 treats the main question as still open: whom will you serve? Joshua names real rivals, the old family gods and the local ones. He gives his own answer first. When the people agree, he pushes back: “You can’t serve the LORD” (verse 19). Verse 23 shows why: foreign gods are still among them. The choice has to be made again by each generation (verse 31).
